Juveniles of the noble crayfish Astacus astacus emerge from the egg at a total length of 0.9 cm , a size measured from the tip of the rostrum to the end of the telson. Following the first moult, which occurs after approximately seven days, the stage 2 juveniles measure 1.2 cm [Lb = 1.2 cm] in total length; they resemble the adult morphology but lack the fully developed tail fan. After an additional three weeks, a further moult yields individuals of 13 to 15 mm, at which point they are considered fully formed. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a weighted average temperature of 10.45 °C [T = 10.45 °C], hatching requires 154 days , while the subsequent first moult, marking the age at birth, occurs seven days thereafter, totalling 161 days [ab = 161 days]. These developmental benchmarks are consistent with the slow, temperature-dependent embryogenesis typical of this species.

Field growth studies conducted at a sustained water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] reveal clear sexual dimorphism in early growth trajectories. By the end of their second summer, female Astacus astacus attain a mean total length of 4.7 cm , whereas their male counterparts reach 4.9 cm  at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This modest advantage in somatic growth among males during the juvenile stage is corroborated by mark-recapture data from Scandinavian populations. The onset of puberty, as defined by the smallest recorded individuals exhibiting gonad maturation, occurs at a total length of 7.7 cm [Lp = 7.7 cm]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 18 grams [Wwp = 18 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. These findings highlight the interplay between thermal regime and sex-specific growth during the formative years.

Reproduction in the noble crayfish is a tightly seasonal event. Under the thermal conditions typical of its native Nordic lakes at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], ovigerous females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year]. The number of attached eggs per clutch ranges from 80 to 200 [N_R_i = 80 to 200], with a mean egg diameter of 2.8 to 3.1 mm. This variation in fecundity is strongly size-dependent: a female of 90 mm total length may carry between 87 and 154 eggs. The maximum lifetime reproductive output is achieved at the ultimate size, with the daily reproduction rate characteristically expressed as one clutch per year. Such an annual cycle imposes selective pressure for optimal timing of the moult and subsequent mating.

Sexual maturation and life span in Astacus astacus show pronounced sex-specific patterns. Females reach puberty at four years since birth [tp = four years since birth] when maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], while males mature more rapidly, attaining puberty at three years since birth [tp = three years since birth] at the same temperature. This earlier maturation in males is likely linked to their faster growth rate and ultimate larger size. The ultimate total length for females is 12 cm [Li = 12 cm], corresponding to a maximum wet weight of 68.2 grams [Wwi = 68.2 grams]; in contrast, males ultimately reach 16 cm [Li = 16 cm] and an adult body mass of 161.5 grams [Wwi = 161.5 grams]. Maximum recorded longevity in this species, under favorable conditions at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], has been reported as 15 years [am = 15 years], although some sources indicate individuals may occasionally persist for over twenty years, particularly in deep, stable lakes where predation pressure is low. The wet weight at birth is extremely low, with the dry weight of newly moulted stage 2 individuals measured at 0.014 grams [Wwb = 0.014 grams], calculated from the approximate volume of a 3 mm diameter egg.

The ecological and physiological context of these measurements underscores the slow life-history strategy of Astacus astacus relative to other European decapods. For instance, the attainment of a total length of 4.7 cm  by females at two years of age at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] represents a growth increment of approximately 3.5 cm from the birth size of 1.2 cm [Lb = 1.2 cm] — a comparatively modest gain that reflects the constraints of cool-water metabolism. The species is further distinguished by a maximum reproductive rate of 1 clutch per year, with the highest fecundity (200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 200 eggs per clutch]) occurring in the largest, oldest females. In contrast, the smallest pubertal females, at 7.7 cm [Lp = 7.7 cm], typically carry only 80 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 80 eggs per clutch]. This fecundity-size relationship is well documented across crayfish populations and has direct implications for fisheries management and conservation strategies aimed at protecting the largest, most fecund individuals.
